source.title: Improving Consistency-Based Semi-Supervised Learning with Weight Averaging
source.authors: Ben Athiwaratkun; Marc Finzi; Pavel Izmailov; A. Wilson

page_placements.theme: Averaging and ensembling have recipe-dependent benefits

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures train and test error along weight-space directions and reports how weight averaging changes test error, using methods and measures different from the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected comparisons, adaptive optimizers, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Its experiments use consistency-based semi-supervised training and weight averaging. The reported ray-geometry and averaging findings are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not match a listed version's specific measure or intervention.
record.test_reason: The study tests consistency regularization and weight averaging, but none of V1–V8. Its direction-specific error-surface widths do not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps. Dropout is a training ingredient without an ablation; switching from published Adam implementations to SGD also changes other training choices and provides no controlled optimizer comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that Π and Mean Teacher training continues exploring diverse solutions late in training, motivating weight averaging. They report improved semi-supervised CIFAR performance with fast-SWA and promising results on CIFAR-10-to-STL domain adaptation.
record.recipe_differences: Consistency-based semi-supervised training with SGD and Nesterov momentum, plus stochastic or fast stochastic weight averaging; it does not use the original interventions or measures in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences by model (Π versus Mean Teacher and supervised training), unlabeled-data quantity, learning-rate schedule and cycle length, averaging frequency, and task; domain adaptation benefited more from per-iteration than per-epoch averaging.

fits_no_version.finding: Late iterates disagree on 7.1% and 6.1% of test examples for Π and Mean Teacher, versus 3.9% for supervised training. Their error surfaces are wider along SGD-to-SGD directions, but comparable along random and adversarial rays.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Consistency-based semi-supervised training sustains diverse late-training predictions and produces direction-dependent differences in solution width.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging late pairs of consistency-model weights reduces test error by 1.2 ± 0.2 percentage points; prediction ensembling reduces it by 0.9 ± 0.2. Prediction diversity correlates with ensemble benefit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Averaging late SGD solutions improves test performance in consistency-based semi-supervised models.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding unlabeled data improves Π-model test accuracy monotonically while solutions become narrower along random rays.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Better semi-supervised test accuracy can coexist with narrower solutions measured along unscaled random weight-space rays.

record.problems: The listed experiments concern semi-supervised consistency training and weight averaging, so they do not directly address most claim versions. Some geometry results are figure-based, and the ray-width measure is direction-specific. The prediction-diversity comparison is an explicitly stated number without reported uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Figure-based sweeps in Figures 4–11 and detailed benchmark tables primarily report semi-supervised or domain-adaptation test errors for the paper’s proposed averaging method, rather than results matching a listed version. The paper reports CNN repeat variability in appendix tables but does not state it for every result in the main figures.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fixed-random-label training, memorization capacity, and held-out accuracy under both label conditions.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons under specified tuning budgets. Published Adam results and the study's altered SGD implementations do not isolate optimizer effects.
Small versus large batches under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Adding or removing dropout, varying dropout strength or training-set size, and jointly removing dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, their association with generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Identifying highly memorized training examples, removing them, and comparing retraining accuracy against matched random removal.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is warranted. The narrower-ray finding does not challenge V7 because it uses a different sharpness measure and does not establish the specified generalization-gap comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and tuning regimes.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout comparisons and interaction with augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation sharpness and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing and retraining after removal of memorized examples.

relation.reason: The paper discusses flatness and generalization, but its experiments do not test the listed versions. Dropout is an ingredient without an ablation, and replacing published Adam implementations with SGD does not provide a controlled optimizer comparison.

tranche.reason: The study investigates consistency regularization and weight averaging without testing or using the specific findings in V1–V8. Its directional error-surface widths do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or ranking of generalization gaps.

source_check.notes: The supplied text's title is There Are Many Consistent Explanations of Unlabeled Data: Why You Should Average, differing from the pack's title. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; the listed results fit none of V1–V8.

statements.correction: Section 3.3: random within-run checkpoint pairs from epochs 180, 183, …, 330; aggregate over Π and MT pairs; reductions relative to mean constituent test error: weight averaging 1.2 ± 0.2 percentage points, prediction ensembling 0.9 ± 0.2 percentage points.
